levels.title: The neck and note names
levels.blurb: String names, the musical alphabet, natural notes on the E and A strings, octave shapes.

hear.text: These are the six open strings, from the lowest sound to the highest.

cards.text: Strings are numbered 6 to 1: string 6 is the thickest and lowest, string 1 the thinnest and highest.
From 6 to 1 the names are E A D G B E. Try: "Eddie Ate Dynamite, Good Bye Eddie."
Playing a string without pressing a fret is an open string. That counts as fret 0.

see.text: Watch and listen: open strings 6 to 1.

tasks.prompt: Tap the open A string.
Tap the open G string.
Tap string 6, fret 5.

play.text: Pick up your guitar. Play the open strings from 6 to 1, one per click, and say each name out loud: E, A, D, G, B, E.

questions.prompt: Which string is number 5?
Tap the open D string.
Tap string 1, open.
What fret number is an open string?

hear.text: Seven letters, then the first one again: A B C D E F G A.

cards.text: Music uses seven letters, A to G. After G it starts again at A.
Most letters are two frets apart, like A and B.
B to C and E to F are only one fret apart. There is no note between them.

see.text: The letters on the low E string, from E up to E again. Watch for the one-fret steps.

tasks.prompt: Tap B on the A string.
Tap the letter after E on the low E string.

Tap D on the A string.

hear.text: Half steps first (one fret each), then whole steps (two frets each).

cards.text: A half step is one fret.
A whole step is two frets.
B to C and E to F are half steps. Every other pair of letters is a whole step.

see.text: On the D string: D to E is a whole step, E to F a half step, F to G a whole step.

lessons.title: Natural notes on the E and A strings

hear.text: The natural notes on the low E string, open to fret 12.

cards.text: These are the letter notes on the low E string. Learn them first: they help you find everything else.
And on the A string, starting from A.
Landmarks help: fret 5 is A on the low E string and D on the A string, fret 7 is B and E, and fret 12 is the open note again.

see.text: The A string, A to A. Say each name as it lights.

cards.text: From the low E or A string: skip a string and go two frets up. Same note, one octave higher.
From the D or G string, the B string shifts it: skip a string and go three frets up.
The low E and high e strings have the same notes at the same frets.

hear.text: A, then A sharp, then B: one fret at a time.

cards.text: Sharp (#) means one fret higher. One fret above A is A#.
Flat (b) means one fret lower. One fret below B is Bb.
So A# and Bb are one fret with two names. Every fret between two letters works this way: C# is Db, F# is Gb.

see.text: Every fret on the A string from A to D, sharps and flats included.

hear.text: Every natural note from the open low E up to fret 3 of the high e: the open position.

cards.text: The open position is frets 0 to 3. Most first chords and melodies live here.
Each string has two or three natural notes here. Learn them string by string, low to high.
The same letters come back higher up. Here are all the E notes in the open position.

levels.title: The major scale and keys
levels.blurb: Build the major scale from whole and half steps, then move it to any key.

hear.text: The G major scale, up one string. You know this sound: do re mi fa so la ti do.

cards.text: A major scale is seven notes and then the first note again. The steps between them always follow one pattern.
The pattern is W W H W W W H: whole, whole, half, whole, whole, whole, half.
The two half steps come after the 3rd note and after the 7th. In G those are B to C and F# to G.

see.text: G major on the low E string. Count the frets between the lights: 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1.

tasks.prompt: Start on G. Tap the note one whole step up.
Keep going: tap the 4th note of G major (a half step after B).
Tap the note that ends the pattern, G again.

play.text: Play G major up the low E string and back down, one note per click. Sing along if you like.

questions.prompt: Which is the major scale pattern?
options: W W H W W W H
W H W W H W W
W W W H W W H
questions.answer: W W H W W W H

questions.prompt: In G major, tap the note after B.
Tap F# on the low E string.
Tap B on the low E string.

hear.text: G major again, now in one small shape across three strings.

cards.text: Root on the low E string: two notes there, three on the A string, three on the D string.
Root on the A string: the same shape, one string higher. This one is C major.
Both shapes start and end on the root, so you always know where you are.

see.text: Up and down the G major shape.

tasks.prompt: In the G major shape, tap the note after A.
Tap the last note of the shape, the high G.
Start a C major shape: tap the C on the A string.

play.text: Play the G major shape up and down. Use one finger per fret: fingers 1 to 4 cover frets 2 to 5.

questions.prompt: In the C major shape, tap the note after C.
Tap the last note of the C major shape.

Tap B in the G major shape.

hear.text: A G drone, then the scale on top. Listen to how the root feels like home.

cards.text: Each note has a number, its scale degree. The root is degree 1, and we write it R.
The root, 3rd and 5th matter most. Together they make the key's main chord.
Numbers work in every key. In G the 3rd is B, and in C the 3rd is E.

see.text: The G major shape with its degree numbers, over a G drone.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 5th of G major.
tasks.explain: Yes! The 5th of G major is D.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 3rd of G major.
tasks.explain: Yes! The 3rd of G major is B.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 6th of G major.
tasks.explain: Yes! The 6th of G major is E.

questions.prompt: Tap the 4th of G major.
Tap the 7th of G major.

lessons.title: Moving the shape to any key

hear.text: G major, then the same shape two frets higher: A major.

cards.text: Slide the whole shape up two frets and it becomes A major.
Put the root on any note of the low E or A string, and the shape gives that major scale. This is D major.
So find the root first, then lay the shape on it.

see.text: A major, root on the low E string at fret 5.

tasks.prompt: Tap the root of A major on the low E string.
Tap the 3rd of A major in this shape.
tasks.explain: Yes! The 3rd of A major is C#.

tasks.prompt: Tap the root of D major on the A string.

hear.text: G major, then the same notes starting from E. Hear how it turns darker.

cards.text: Play the notes of G major starting on its 6th note, E, and you get E minor.
Every major key has a relative minor that shares all its notes. Its root is three frets below the major root.
From E, the degrees are 1 2 b3 4 5 b6 b7. The flat 3rd is what makes it sound minor.

see.text: E minor over an E drone.

hear.text: The G major pentatonic: five notes that sound open and happy.

cards.text: Take the 4th and 7th out of the major scale. The five notes left are the major pentatonic.
With no half steps left, every note sounds good over the key's chord. That makes it great for first solos.
This box covers all six strings of G major pentatonic, frets 2 to 5.

see.text: Up and down the G major pentatonic box.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 2nd of G major pentatonic.

hear.text: The minor pentatonic, then a first blues lick made from it.

cards.text: Play G major pentatonic from its relative minor, E, and you have E minor pentatonic: the same five notes.
Its degrees are 1 b3 4 5 b7. Box 1 puts the root under your first finger on the low E string: at fret 5 it is A minor pentatonic.
Your first blues lick: G, E, D, C, then home to A.

levels.title: Intervals
levels.blurb: Hear and find distances from the root: 3rds, 5ths, octaves and more.

hear.text: C, then E. C, then G. C, then C an octave up. Three distances from one root.

cards.text: An interval is the distance from the root to another note.
We name it by the scale degree it lands on. C to E is a 3rd, and C to G is a 5th.
Count the root as 1. C, D, E is three letters, so C to E is a 3rd.

see.text: Every degree of C major, named as an interval from C.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 3rd above this C.
tasks.explain: Yes! That's the major 3rd: E.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 5th above this C.
tasks.explain: Yes! That's the perfect 5th: G.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 2nd above this C.
tasks.explain: Yes! The 2nd above C is D.

play.text: Play root, 3rd, 5th, 3rd from C, and say the names as you go: "root, three, five, three".

cards.text: The 3rd: one string up, one fret back.
The 5th: one string up, two frets up. The octave: two strings up, two frets up.
Crossing onto the B string, every shape moves one fret higher.

cards.text: A major 3rd is 4 frets above the root. It sounds bright.
A minor 3rd is 3 frets above the root, written b3. It sounds darker.
On the neck, the major 3rd is one string up and one fret back. The minor 3rd is two frets back.

cards.text: A perfect 4th is 5 frets up: the same fret on the next string.
A perfect 5th is 7 frets up: next string, two frets up.
Root and 5th together (often with the octave) is a power chord, written G5.

cards.text: A drone holds the root under everything. Each degree has its own feeling against it.
The root sounds like home, the 5th strong and open, the 3rd sweet.

levels.title: Chords and CAGED
levels.blurb: Triads from 1-3-5, the chords in a key, and the five CAGED shapes.

hear.text: C, E and G one at a time, then all together: the C major chord.

cards.text: A chord is three or more notes played together. The simplest, a triad, is the root, 3rd and 5th.
Take every other note of the scale: C, skip D, E, skip F, G.
Play them together and you hear the C major chord. The open C chord is just those three notes, repeated.

see.text: The open C chord, note by note, then strummed.

tasks.prompt: Tap the 3rd of the C major chord.
tasks.explain: Yes! The 3rd of C major is E.

tasks.prompt: Tap the root of the G major chord.
tasks.explain: Yes! G is the root.

hear.text: G major, G minor, then G diminished. Bright, sad, then tense.

cards.text: A major triad is the root, a major 3rd and a perfect 5th. It sounds bright.
Lower the 3rd one fret to b3 and it becomes minor. It sounds sad.
Lower the 5th as well, to b5, and it is diminished. It sounds tense.

The pattern is the same in every major key: major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished.
Roman numerals name the chords by degree. Upper case is major, lower case is minor.

Move each note up to the next chord tone and you get the same chord in a new shape.
Three shapes cover the neck: around frets 3, 7 and 12. Each one has the root in a different place.

cards.text: Barre an open E shape with your first finger and it slides anywhere. At fret 5 it is A major.
Every major chord can be played with five open-chord shapes: C, A, G, E and D. That is CAGED.
In each shape the root is your anchor. Find the root and you have the chord, like this A-shape C.

lessons.title: The minor pentatonic in five positions

hear.text: A minor pentatonic, position 1: the sound of a thousand rock solos.

cards.text: The minor pentatonic has five notes: 1 b3 4 5 b7. Position 1 in A sits at frets 5 to 8.
Four more positions join it up the neck, each starting where the last one ends.
Each position wraps around a shape of the A minor chord. Position 1 holds the E-shape Am.
